## Hands-on 4 – Exploring the menu {#hands-on-4-work-the-menu .smaller}

::: {.small}
**Task 4 is exploratory.** Try several specifications, look at what each one does, and get a feel for which decisions move the estimate.

1. Start from the reproduced specification, the model of C6HJR, which every argument of `try_spec()` takes as its default
2. Change **one decision** in `try_spec()` and read what happens to *b*, the partial *r*, the CR2 p and the placement; `my_experiments()` lists every try
3. Do it again with a different decision. Three or four is plenty, and one option that is off the curve, to read why it is refused
4. Then rerun the one you can argue for best with `try_spec()`, so that it is your last try, and **submit it** with `submit_exploration()`
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Your dot appears on the live **Class results** page within seconds, and we read the dots from the whole class once everyone has submitted.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
This is **not** your preregistered analysis. You are allowed to look, change your mind and try again, which is why this phase has a name of its own.
:::

::: notes
Task 4 is exploration, which differs from the preregistered analysis that comes later. Start from the reproduced specification, my own model, which every argument of `try_spec()` takes as its default. Change one decision and read what happens to the coefficient, the partial r, the CR2 p-value and the placement, then do it again with a different decision, three or four tries in all, with one option off the curve, such as pooled OLS, to read the reason for its refusal; `my_experiments()` lists the tries. Then rerun the try for which you can argue best, so that it is your last, and submit it with `submit_exploration()`. [advance] Your dot appears on the Class results page within seconds. [advance] Here, unlike in the preregistration, you may look, change your mind and try again, and most published work never says that such a phase took place, which is why it has a name of its own.
:::
